items.abstract: <jats:p>State-owned development banks play a pivotal role in financing structural transformation, yet the microeconomic friction they introduce into incumbent commercial banking sectors remains theoretically underexplored, particularly in small open economies. This paper develops a partial-equilibrium banking model to assess how development bank (DB) lending influences the commercial intermediation spread, linking the model to a production possibilities frontier subject to a foreign exchange constraint. We numerically simulate the framework for 14 small open economies with existing development banks. Three findings emerge. First, DB interventions are not universally complementary; their effect depends on the host economy’s bank liquidity regime, widening the spread through an implicit-tax mechanism in high bank liquidity environments and compressing it through a funding-cost mechanism. Second, the model uncovers a partial-equilibrium paradox in which a development bank that successfully finances export-oriented sectors generates a foreign exchange gain that paradoxically widens the domestic spread, as commercial banks reprice the opportunity cost of the safe foreign asset. Third, a portfolio-rebalancing channel toward government securities produces a genuinely mixed effect across the sample, compressing the spread where the domestic Treasury bill rate exceeds the foreign risk-free rate and widening it otherwise.</jats:p>
title: Development Banking, Intermediation Spread, and the Foreign Exchange Constraint in Small Open Economies

items.abstract: <jats:p>There is growing interest in state-owned development banks (DBs) as a source of finance for structural transformation. However, the microeconomic friction these state-capitalized institutions introduce into domestic commercial banking sectors remains theoretically underexplored, particularly in the context of open economies. This paper addresses this gap by developing a banking model to assess how DB loan and deposit spillovers impact the commercial intermediation spread. Recognizing the binding nature of the balance of payments, we link this imperfectly competitive banking model (partial equilibrium) with a general-equilibrium production possibilities curve (PPC) to capture foreign exchange (FX) constraints. We numerically simulate the framework using data from 14 small open economies. The analysis yields two main findings. First, DB interventions are not universally complementary; their impact depends on the host economy&apos;s bank liquidity condition. In high bank liquidity environments, non-remunerated DB deposit spillovers act as an implicit tax, crowding out private credit by widening the commercial intermediation spread. Conversely, normal liquidity regimes experience spread compression, crowding in commercial lending. Second, the model uncovers a partial-equilibrium paradox: when a DB successfully finances export-oriented sectors, generating a net FX gain that expands the macroeconomic production frontier, commercial banks (at the micro level) paradoxically widen the domestic spread to compensate for the higher opportunity cost of the safe foreign asset.</jats:p>
title: Development Banking, Intermediation Spread, and the Foreign Exchange Constraint in Small Open Economies
